title: Expense Tracker
story: Where did all your money go? That question has haunted humans since the invention of currency. Now you build the answer. Log every coffee, bus fare, movie ticket, and impulse purchase. Categorize them: Food, Transport, Entertainment, Bills. See exactly where your money flows with category summaries and percentages. Find the biggest expense — the one that made you wince. Add a monthly budget, and watch the tracker warn you when you're about to overspend. This is personal finance, engineered by you.
why: The Expense Tracker combines structs for transactions, enums for categories, Vec for transaction history, Map for category aggregation, and budget alert logic — a complete personal finance tool demonstrating data entry, analysis, and reporting.
analogy: A checkbook register meets a pie chart. Every time you spend money, you write it in the register: date, description, amount, category. At month's end, you add up each category column: 'I spent $347 on Food, $120 on Transport, $89 on Entertainment.' The pie chart (your category summary) shows where your money went at a glance. The budget line is a red marker — cross it, and alarms go off.
try_it: Add monthly budget tracking with alerts: if spending hits 50%, 80%, 100% of budget, print yellow/orange/red warnings. Add date tracking (day/month) and filter expenses by month. Calculate average daily spend. Add export to a 'CSV' format: name,amount,category per line. Add an 'income' type to track money coming in vs going out.
tips: Store amounts in cents (integers) to avoid floating-point weirdness — $12.50 = 1250
Category totals are calculated by filtering expenses by category enum, then summing amounts
Budget check runs after every expense add — real-time feedback prevents overspending
common_mistakes: Forgetting to initialize Vec with .new() before pushing expenses
Category comparison must use == on enum values, not string comparison on category names
Biggest expense finder crashes on empty ledger — check len() > 0 first
